analysis.one_liner: Designates the Arctic refuge coastal plain as wilderness, permanently banning oil drilling there.
analysis.headline: The bill had 145 cosponsors, including 3 Republicans, but never got a hearing or a vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make about 1.56 million acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain — an area left unprotected when Congress set the refuge's other lands aside in 1980 — part of the National Wilderness Preservation System. Wilderness designation is the strongest protection federal law offers: no roads, no mining, and no oil and gas drilling, permanently. The bill says subsistence hunting and gathering by local residents would continue as allowed under existing refuge law.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who value unspoiled public lands, future generations who would inherit the coastal plain undisturbed, the wildlife — including the Porcupine River caribou herd — that depends on the plain for calving grounds, and Alaska Native communities that rely on subsistence uses the bill expressly preserves.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Conservation-minded public and Alaska Native subsistence users

how_it_helps.text: Designates roughly 1,559,538 acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain as wilderness under the Wilderness Act, the strictest land protection in federal law [S2] [S3].
The bill states the coastal plain would remain managed for continued subsistence uses by local residents, as required by the 1980 law establishing the refuge [S3].

The bill's findings note that a majority of Americans support protecting the refuge from industrial development, and that wilderness protection would still leave most of Alaska's North Slope open to energy development [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose access to what is believed to be one of the largest undeveloped onshore petroleum prospects in the United States, and Alaska loses potential revenue, jobs, and royalties from coastal plain development.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies and Alaska

drawbacks.text: Wilderness designation is permanent, so the bill would foreclose drilling on the coastal plain — by industry estimates a significant oil and gas resource — for good, whatever future energy prices or security needs look like [S3].

Alaska's economy and state revenues depend heavily on resource development, and the bill's sponsors argue the rest of the North Slope remains open; opponents of wilderness designations in Alaska contend the state gives up more than its share [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is permanent and the habitat it covers — calving grounds for a caribou herd that migrates through both the U.S. and Canada — cannot be restored once industrialized. The cost falls on a single concentrated industry and on Alaska's development-dependent economy, while most of the North Slope stays open to drilling. The main honest objection is the irreversibility: if circumstances changed, wilderness designation leaves no way to revisit the choice.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to a subcommittee, and the committee never acted on it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Huffman introduced the bill on April 4, 2017, joined by original cosponsors Reps. Fitzpatrick, LoBiondo, and Gallego [S1] [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources and, a week later, to its Subcommittee on Federal Lands; no further action was recorded for the rest of the 115th Congress [S5].
It gathered 145 cosponsors — 142 Democrats and 3 Republicans — but never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas interests and officials who wanted the coastal plain kept open for drilling were better off, since wilderness designation never came to a vote. In late 2017, the same Congress instead opened the coastal plain to oil and gas leasing through the tax reform act, the opposite of this bill's goal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas interests kept the plain open

sides.party_line_note: Of the bill's 145 cosponsors, 142 were Democrats and only 3 were Republicans; no committee or floor vote was ever taken, so the full House never weighed in.

industries.note: Wilderness designation would permanently bar drilling on the coastal plain, which the industry has sought for decades as one of the largest undeveloped onshore oil prospects in the U.S. Its interest in keeping the plain open runs directly against the conservation outcome the bill offers the public.
The state would forgo jobs, royalties, and revenue tied to coastal plain development. The bill's counterargument is that most of Alaska's North Slope would remain open to energy production [S3].
Permanent wilderness protection preserves the undisturbed landscape that guides, outfitters, and visitors rely on.
